questions.prompt: Which statements are true?

options.A: For x<y real, some r∈ℚ has x<2²⁰²⁴r/e<y
options.B: If positive a_n satisfies limsup a_n/log n=L>0 finite, then limsup a_n<∞
options.C: The set of all finite subsets of ℚ is countably infinite
options.D: The set of continuous functions ℝ→{0,1} is infinite

hints: Scale the interval in A before applying density of ℚ.
For B use a_n=log n; for D use connectedness of ℝ.
questions.solution: A holds because density of ℚ supplies r between ex/2²⁰²⁴ and ey/2²⁰²⁴. B fails for a_n=log n: the normalized limsup is 1 but a_n→∞. For C, finite subsets of cardinality k are images of the countable set ℚᵏ; the union over k≥0 is countable and contains infinitely many singleton subsets. D fails because a continuous image of connected ℝ is connected, so the only functions into {0,1} are the two constants. Exactly A,C are true.
questions.theory: A set is countable if it is finite or admits an enumeration by natural numbers. Finite products and countable unions of countable sets are countable. Therefore the family of finite subsets of a countable set is countable: enumerate subsets by their finite cardinality and use tuples as a countable covering family. A subset of ℝ is dense if every nonempty open interval contains one of its points; nonzero scalar multiples of the rational numbers are dense. Continuous images of connected spaces are connected, so a continuous map from ℝ into the discrete set {0,1} is constant. Limsup describes tail behavior and need not bound an original sequence when a growing normalization is used. Common pitfalls include confusing countability with density and assuming a normalized bounded sequence must itself be bounded.

similar_questions.prompt: Is the family of finite subsets of ℤ countable?
similar_questions.solution: Yes. For each k it is covered by ℤᵏ, which is countable. A countable union of these families is countable; infinitely many singleton subsets make it countably infinite.

similar_questions.prompt: How many continuous maps from [0,1] to {−1,1} exist?
similar_questions.solution: [0,1] is connected and the target is discrete. Its continuous image must be a singleton, so only the two constant maps exist.

questions.prompt: a_n=(−1)ⁿ(1+e⁻ⁿ), b_n=max{a₁,…,a_n}, c_n=min{a₁,…,a_n}. Which are true?
hints: Separate the even and odd subsequences.
Running extrema retain early exceptional terms; tail extrema do not.
questions.solution: Even terms tend to 1 and odd terms to −1, so a_n diverges and A is true. The largest positive term is a₂=1+e⁻², and b_n equals this for n≥2. The most negative term is a₁=−1−e⁻¹, and c_n equals this for all n. Yet limsup a_n=1 and liminf a_n=−1. Thus B,C fail, and the limits of b_n,c_n are unequal, rejecting D.
questions.theory: A sequence is bounded above if one real number exceeds all its terms, and unbounded above if for every real x some term exceeds x. These quantifiers are central: an unbounded-above sequence need not be unbounded below. Exponential growth eⁿ dominates its reciprocal e⁻ⁿ as n tends to infinity. For positive sequences, ratios aₙ₊₁/aₙ can remain bounded even when aₙ diverges to infinity. To analyze a ratio containing exponentials, divide numerator and denominator by the dominant exponential. A limiting value alone does not establish a bound for every n; an explicit algebraic inequality can do so. Common pitfalls include confusing the growth of a sequence with the growth of its consecutive ratio and forgetting that a positive sequence cannot lie below every real number.

similar_questions.prompt: For a_n=1/n, compare running maximum and limsup.
similar_questions.solution: The running maximum is always a₁=1, while limsup a_n=0. The difference is the retention of the first term in the running maximum.

similar_questions.prompt: For a_n=(−1)ⁿ, find running and tail extrema.
similar_questions.solution: Even values are 1 and odd values −1. For n≥2 the running maximum is 1 and minimum −1; limsup=1, liminf=−1. Equality occurs here because the extreme values recur indefinitely.

questions.prompt: f(x)=x²sin(1/x) for x≠0, f(0)=0. Which are true?
hints: Bound the oscillatory expression by x².
Use the derivative definition at zero and then differentiate away from zero.
questions.solution: |f(x)|≤x²→0, proving existence of the limit and continuity. The zero difference quotient is f(h)/h=h sin(1/h)→0, so f′(0)=0. For x≠0, f′(x)=2x sin(1/x)−cos(1/x). At x_k=1/(2πk), this is −1; at y_k=1/((2k+1)π), it is +1. Both tend to zero, so f′ has no limit there. All A,B,C,D are true.
questions.theory: Differentiability at a point is defined by a limit of difference quotients in one dimension, and by a linear approximation with error o(‖h‖) in several dimensions. Differentiability implies continuity. Existence of all partial derivatives or even every directional derivative does not imply total differentiability. Oscillatory factors such as sin(1/x) can be controlled by |sin|≤1 to establish continuity or a first derivative at zero, but their differentiated expressions can retain nonvanishing oscillation. To disprove a multivariable limit, compare two paths; curved paths can reveal behavior invisible on all straight lines. If a total derivative exists, its coefficients must agree with the partial derivatives. Common pitfalls include differentiating a formula only valid away from the point and assigning its limiting derivative without evaluating the actual definition.

similar_questions.prompt: Analyze differentiability at zero of x³sin(1/x), extended by zero.
similar_questions.solution: The quotient x²sin(1/x) tends to zero, so the derivative at zero is 0. Away from zero its derivative is 3x²sin(1/x)−x cos(1/x), which tends to 0; the derivative is continuous at zero.

similar_questions.prompt: Analyze x sin(1/x), extended by zero.
similar_questions.solution: Its absolute value is at most |x|, so it is continuous at zero. Its difference quotient is sin(1/x), which has no limit, so it is not differentiable there.

questions.prompt: f_n(x)=nx(1−x)ⁿ on [0,1]. Which are true?

options.B: Pointwise convergence to a continuous function
options.C: Pointwise convergence to a discontinuous function

hints: For fixed interior x, exponential decay beats n.
Evaluate the maximum at x=1/(n+1).
questions.solution: At x=0,1 every term is zero. For 0<x<1, n(1−x)ⁿ→0, so the pointwise limit is identically zero and continuous, giving B and rejecting A,C. Differentiating yields f_n′=n(1−x)^(n−1)[1−(n+1)x], so the maximum is f_n(1/(n+1))=(n/(n+1))^(n+1)→e⁻¹, not zero. The supremum error does not vanish, proving D.
questions.theory: Pointwise convergence of functions means that for each fixed x the numerical sequence converges; uniform convergence requires one index controlling the error simultaneously at every point of the domain. For a series, absolute convergence means convergence of the series of absolute values at each point. Uniform convergence of continuous functions preserves continuity, which provides an efficient obstruction when the proposed limit is discontinuous. A geometric series ∑rⁿ converges to 1/(1−r) exactly when |r|<1. Endpoints where the multiplier vanishes must be examined separately rather than cancelled. The uniform Cauchy criterion tests tails in the supremum norm. Common pitfalls include exchanging a pointwise limit with another limit, treating pointwise absolute convergence as uniform convergence, and using the Weierstrass M-test as a necessary rather than sufficient condition.

similar_questions.prompt: Does n x²(1−x)ⁿ converge uniformly to zero?
similar_questions.solution: The maximum occurs at x=2/(n+2). Its value is n·4/(n+2)²·(n/(n+2))ⁿ≤4n/(n+2)²→0, so convergence is uniform.

similar_questions.prompt: Does (1−x)ⁿ converge uniformly on [0,1]?
similar_questions.solution: Its pointwise limit is 1 at zero and 0 elsewhere, which is discontinuous. Continuous summands cannot converge uniformly to that limit.

questions.prompt: f:ℝ→ℝ is continuous and zero for x≤0 and x≥1. F(x)=∑_{n∈ℤ}f(x+n). Which are true?

options.C: F is uniformly continuous on ℝ
options.D: F is not uniformly continuous on ℝ

hints: At each noninteger point, at most one summand is nonzero.
The sum is continuous and periodic with period one.
questions.solution: For x∈(k,k+1), F(x)=f(x−k). At integers all terms vanish because f(0)=f(1)=0. Thus successive copies join continuously. Reindexing gives F(x+1)=F(x). Since f is bounded on [0,1], F is bounded. Continuity and periodicity imply uniform continuity by applying Heine–Cantor on, for example, [−1,2] and reducing arguments by a common integer. Therefore A,B,C hold and D fails.
questions.theory: A continuous function with compact support is bounded and uniformly continuous. Periodization sums its integer translates; if support lies in a compact interval then only finitely many translates contribute in any bounded neighborhood. Such a locally finite sum is continuous. Reindexing the translates shows period one. A continuous periodic function is bounded and uniformly continuous, since one can reduce the relevant points to a compact interval containing a fundamental period and neighboring periods, then apply the Heine–Cantor theorem. For support inside [0,1], at most one translate is nonzero at any particular noninteger point, and endpoint vanishing joins successive copies continuously. Common pitfalls include applying convergence tests to a sum that is locally finite and assuming continuity alone on the unbounded real line implies uniform continuity.

similar_questions.prompt: Periodize f(x)=x(1−x) on [0,1], zero outside. Find its maximum.
similar_questions.solution: The periodized function is {x}(1−{x}) on each unit interval, with zero at integers. Its maximum is 1/4 at half-integers; it is continuous and uniformly continuous.

similar_questions.prompt: Why would periodizing f≡1 on (0,1), with f=0 at endpoints, fail continuity?
similar_questions.solution: The base function itself jumps at its endpoints. The periodized result is 1 at nonintegers and 0 at integers, so jumps persist; continuity of the original f is essential.

questions.prompt: g is continuous on ℝ and f(x)=∫₀ˣ(x−t)g(t)dt. Which are true?

options.D: f″(0) exists but differs from g(0)

hints: Differentiate with the variable-endpoint Leibniz rule.
The endpoint term vanishes because x−t=0 at t=x.
questions.solution: f(0)=0. Leibniz gives f′(x)=∫₀ˣg(t)dt+(x−x)g(x)=∫₀ˣg(t)dt. Thus f′(0)=0. By the fundamental theorem of calculus, f″(x)=g(x), in particular f″(0)=g(0). A,B,C are true and D is false.
questions.theory: The fundamental theorem of calculus says that if g is continuous, then G(x)=∫₀ˣg(t)dt is differentiable and G′(x)=g(x), including for negative x through oriented integration. An integral with a variable endpoint and a parameter-dependent integrand is differentiated by the Leibniz rule: endpoint contribution plus the integral of the parameter derivative. This often creates higher smoothness than the original integrand has. Monotone real functions on a compact interval are bounded and Riemann integrable; their discontinuities are jump discontinuities and form a countable set. Monotone functions are Borel measurable because preimages of rays are intervals, and Borel measurability implies Lebesgue measurability. Common pitfalls include demanding a derivative of g when only its continuity is needed and overlooking the difference between countably many discontinuities and a discontinuity at every point.

similar_questions.prompt: If g(t)=1, evaluate f and its first two derivatives.
similar_questions.solution: f=∫₀ˣ(x−t)dt=x²/2, f′=x and f″=1=g. At zero f=f′=0.

similar_questions.prompt: If g(t)=t, evaluate f.
similar_questions.solution: f=x∫₀ˣt dt−∫₀ˣt²dt=x³/2−x³/3=x³/6. Hence f′=x²/2 and f″=x=g(x).

similar_questions.prompt: For f(x)=1_{x≥1/2}, decide integrability and measurability.

similar_questions.prompt: Give a monotone function with infinitely many discontinuities.

questions.prompt: X={u∈C[0,1]:u(0)=0}, ‖u‖=sup|u|. T(u)=∫₀¹u(t)dt and S={|T(u)|:u∈X,‖u‖≤1}. Which are true?
hints: Bound the integral by the sup norm.
Continuity at zero prevents equality, but narrow boundary ramps approach it.
questions.solution: |T(u)|≤∫|u|≤1, so S is bounded. Since u(0)=0 and u is continuous, for some δ>0, |u|≤1/2 on [0,δ], giving |T(u)|≤1−δ/2<1; the bound is never attained. Let u_n(t)=min(nt,1). Then u_n∈X, ‖u_n‖=1 and T(u_n)=1−1/(2n)→1. Thus sup S=1 but 1∉S; S is not closed. In fact scaling these functions yields every value in [0,1). Only B is true.
questions.theory: A normed-space linear functional T is bounded when |T(u)|≤C‖u‖ for a finite constant C; its operator norm is the least such C, equivalently the supremum over the unit ball. A supremum need not be attained. For an integration functional on continuous functions, |∫u|≤∫|u|≤‖u‖ gives an upper bound. Extra constraints such as u(0)=0 can prevent equality, because continuity forces a nontrivial interval where |u| is strictly below one. Nevertheless functions rising rapidly from zero to one can approach the upper bound arbitrarily closely. A bounded image of a closed unit ball need not be closed in infinite dimensions. Common pitfalls include equating norm one with existence of a maximizing vector and using finite-dimensional compactness for an infinite-dimensional unit ball.

similar_questions.prompt: On all of C[0,1], does the integration functional attain norm one?
similar_questions.solution: Yes. The constant function u≡1 has norm one and integral one. Removing the constraint u(0)=0 permits a maximizer.

similar_questions.prompt: Compute the integral of u_n(t)=min(nt,1).
similar_questions.solution: Split at 1/n: ∫₀^(1/n)nt dt+∫_(1/n)¹1dt=1/(2n)+1−1/n=1−1/(2n). Its values approach one strictly from below.

questions.prompt: V consists of real polynomials of degree ≤3. D is differentiation and M(f)=xD(f). Which are true?
hints: Apply each operator to xᵏ.
Constants are killed, while DM and MD differ on x.
questions.solution: For k=0,1,2,3, M(xᵏ)=kxᵏ. Thus DM(xᵏ)=k²x^(k−1), while MD(xᵏ)=k(k−1)x^(k−1), proving DM−MD=D≠0. Constants are killed by D+M and DM, so neither is invertible. DM has image span{1,x,x²}, rank 3; MD has image span{x,x²}, rank 2. Hence only A holds.
questions.theory: For a linear operator T, a polynomial p(T) is defined by substituting the operator into the polynomial and using composition for powers. The identity operator I commutes with every operator, so ordinary polynomial identities remain valid for T and I. On polynomials of degree at most m, differentiation D is nilpotent: D^(m+1)=0. Thus T=I+D can simplify high powers or polynomial combinations without expanding thousands of compositions. For a matrix satisfying A³=I, the roots of its minimal polynomial are among cube roots of unity; because those roots are distinct over the complex numbers, the matrix is diagonalizable there. Nevertheless rank conclusions can also be proved directly by factorizations. Common pitfalls include treating an operator power as multiplication of function values and overlooking a low-degree annihilating polynomial.

similar_questions.prompt: Compute the commutator [D,M] on arbitrary differentiable f.
similar_questions.solution: DMf=D(xf′)=f′+xf″ and MDf=xD(f′)=xf″. Their difference is f′, so [D,M]=D.

similar_questions.prompt: On degree-at-most-two polynomials, compute ranks of DM and MD.
similar_questions.solution: DM sends x to 1 and x² to 4x, so its image span{1,x} has rank 2. MD kills x and sends x² to 2x, so its rank is 1.

questions.prompt: V is the ℚ-space of polynomials of degree ≤3. A={f:V→ℚ | f linear}, B={f∈A:f(1)=0}. Which are true?

options.A: For every f∈B, dim ker f=3
options.D: For every f∈A, im f has dimension 1

hints: A linear functional is described by its four basis values.
The zero functional must be included in universal claims.
questions.solution: {1,x,x²,x³} is a basis, so dim A=4. B fixes the first basis value to zero and leaves three free values, hence dim B=3. A is false because the zero functional belongs to B and has a four-dimensional kernel. D is false for the same zero functional, whose image has dimension zero. Nonzero functionals do have rank one and kernel dimension three, but the options do not restrict to nonzero f. Thus B,C hold.
questions.theory: A vector space basis is a linearly independent spanning family; its size is the dimension. A linear transformation is determined by its values on a basis. For a finite-dimensional space U, the dual U* of real-valued linear functionals has the same dimension as U, even if U consists of functions in an infinite-dimensional ambient space. Rank–nullity states dim U=rank T+dim ker T. Matrix rank is the dimension of its column space and equals the row rank. The trace is the sum of diagonal entries and satisfies tr(AB)=tr(BA). Orthogonal complements are computed using homogeneous linear equations. Common pitfalls include substituting the dimension of the ambient function space for that of a finite span, confusing a matrix's determinant with rank, and forgetting that a single nontrivial linear constraint reduces dimension by exactly one.

similar_questions.prompt: For a nonzero linear functional on ℚ⁵, find kernel dimension.
similar_questions.solution: Its image is a nonzero subspace of ℚ, hence has dimension 1. Rank–nullity gives kernel dimension 5−1=4.

similar_questions.prompt: For the dual of degree≤4 polynomials, find dimension of functionals vanishing on 1 and x.
similar_questions.solution: The dual has dimension 5; two independent basis-value constraints leave three free coordinates. The constrained space has dimension 3.

questions.solution: g=1/(f−1) is well-defined and holomorphic on the punctured plane, with |g|≤1. Both punctures are removable for g, so g extends to a bounded entire function and is constant by Liouville. On its original domain g never vanishes, so its constant is nonzero and f=1+1/g is constant. Thus f itself extends across both punctures and is bounded. A,B,C hold, while D fails.
questions.theory: Liouville's theorem says that a bounded entire function is constant. The removable-singularity theorem allows a holomorphic function bounded near an isolated missing point to extend holomorphically across it. If the original function omits a disc centered at a, the reciprocal 1/(f−a) is bounded; it can be extended across finitely many punctures and Liouville then forces constancy. A nonconstant complex polynomial grows in modulus to infinity as |z| grows, so inverse images of bounded modulus discs are bounded and open by continuity. Boundary points of a strict sublevel set satisfy equality of the modulus. If a component contained no zero, applying the maximum-modulus principle to 1/P on the component would contradict the smaller boundary modulus. Common pitfalls include applying Liouville directly to an unbounded f and assuming a polynomial sublevel set must be connected.

hints: A nonzero holomorphic f has a finite-order zero at zero.
Along positive real x, e^(1/x)xᵐ grows without bound for every fixed m.
questions.solution: If f were not identically zero, write f(z)=zᵐh(z) with finite m≥0 and h(0)≠0. For small positive x, |h(x)|≥|h(0)|/2, so |g(x)|≥(|h(0)|/2)xᵐe^(1/x)→∞, contradicting boundedness. questions.theory: A holomorphic function near zero has a convergent Taylor series. If it is not identically zero, it has a zero of some finite order m and can be written f(z)=zᵐh(z) with h(0)≠0. An exponential e^(1/z) grows faster than every reciprocal power along the positive real axis, so multiplication by a finite-order zero cannot make it bounded near zero. Rotational symmetry f(iz)=f(z) instead restricts Taylor coefficients: a coefficient of zⁿ can be nonzero only if iⁿ=1, meaning n is divisible by four. Regrouping these terms yields an entire function of z⁴. The regrouped series is entire because its fourth-root argument can be chosen at arbitrary large modulus. Common pitfalls include using essential-singularity intuition without a growth argument and concluding rotational symmetry forces a function to be constant.

In a finite group, a subset larger than half the group intersects every translate of its inverse, so its pairwise product set is the whole group. An evaluation map on a ring of functions is a surjective ring homomorphism to the scalar field; its kernel is maximal and hence prime. Euclidean domains are principal ideal domains, but polynomial rings in two or more variables are not principal ideal domains: the ideal generated by two distinct variables is not principal. Common pitfalls include confusing multivariable polynomial rings with one-variable Euclidean domains and forgetting inverses when proving a product-set pigeonhole argument.

questions.solution: B holds because every ratio lies in [0,1]. Since the ratios sum to |X(n)|/n→1, if all eight upper limits were <1/8, their finite sum would be <1, contradicting limsup of the sum ≤sum of limsups. This proves C and rejects D. A fails: let X=ℕ and put alternating blocks with endpoints N_k=2^(2^k) into X₁,X₂, distributing any finitely many initial integers among the other pieces. questions.theory: The natural density of a subset S of positive integers is the limit, when it exists, of |S∩{1,…,n}|/n. Lower and upper density are the corresponding liminf and limsup and always exist as bounded extended limits in [0,1]. A finite disjoint partition has counting ratios whose sum equals the ratio of the union, but individual limits need not exist even if the sum converges. The sum of finitely many limsups bounds the limsup of their sum from above, so a density-one set partitioned into m pieces has at least one piece with upper density ≥1/m. Alternating blocks with lengths dominating all previous blocks can create oscillation between densities close to zero and one. Common pitfalls include assuming densities distribute equally or exist for every member of a partition.

questions.prompt: R is a nonzero ring with identity and r²=r for every r∈R. Which are true?

options.A: R is never an integral domain
options.C: Every nonzero prime ideal is maximal

hints: Expand (1+1)²=1+1.
Expand (r+s)² and examine prime quotients.
questions.solution: Idempotence of 2·1 gives 4·1=2·1, hence 2·1=0 and 2r=0, proving B. Expanding (r+s)²=r+s and cancelling r²=r,s²=s gives rs+sr=0; since additive negatives equal positives, rs=sr, proving D. For any prime ideal P, R/P is a Boolean domain. Every element t satisfies t(t−1)=0, forcing t=0 or 1, so the quotient is the two-element field and P is maximal; C follows, even for zero prime ideals. A fails because the field 𝔽₂ is a Boolean integral domain.
questions.theory: A Boolean ring is a ring in which every element satisfies r²=r. Expanding (1+1)²=1+1 yields 2·1=0, so the ring has characteristic two and r=−r for every element. Expanding (r+s)²=r+s then gives rs+sr=0, which in characteristic two means rs=sr. Thus every Boolean ring is commutative. A Boolean integral domain is necessarily the two-element field: r(r−1)=0 forces every r to be zero or one. Every prime quotient of a Boolean ring is therefore this field, so each prime ideal is maximal. Nontrivial Boolean rings need not be domains, as a product of two copies of the two-element field shows. Common pitfalls include assuming idempotence means absence of zero divisors and overlooking the two-element field as a counterexample to a universal negative claim.

similar_questions.prompt: Show 𝔽₂×𝔽₂ is Boolean but not a domain.
similar_questions.solution: Each coordinate squares to itself, so every pair is idempotent. Yet (1,0)(0,1)=(0,0) with both factors nonzero, giving zero divisors.

similar_questions.prompt: Find the maximal ideals of 𝔽₂×𝔽₂.
similar_questions.solution: The kernels of the two coordinate projections are {0}×𝔽₂ and 𝔽₂×{0}. Each quotient is 𝔽₂, so both are maximal and prime.

questions.prompt: A group is divisible if every y has an nth root for every positive integer n. Which groups are divisible?
hints: In additive notation an nth root means solving nx=y.
For a finite group choose n equal to the group order.
questions.solution: In (ℚ,+), x=y/n is rational and solves nx=y, so A holds. Every nonzero complex number has an nth root by polar form, so B holds. In C₅, every x satisfies x⁵=e, so a nonidentity y has no fifth root. In S₅, every x satisfies x¹²⁰=e by Lagrange, so a nonidentity y has no 120th root. C,D fail. More generally no nontrivial finite group is divisible.
questions.theory: A finite group of prime order is cyclic by Lagrange's theorem: a nonidentity element generates a subgroup whose order must be the prime. Composite orders can also admit a unique group up to isomorphism. A positive integer n is a cyclic number precisely when gcd(n,φ(n))=1, where φ is Euler's totient; equivalently every group of order n is cyclic exactly under this condition. The obstruction is constructive: if p² divides n, two nonisomorphic abelian groups of order n can be formed; if n is squarefree and p divides q−1 for primes p,q dividing n, a nonabelian semidirect product of order pq exists. Group counts grow without bound along prime powers because distinct partitions give distinct finite abelian groups. Common pitfalls include extending the prime-order theorem to an “only if” statement and counting only abelian groups.

similar_questions.prompt: Is (ℝ,+) divisible?
similar_questions.solution: Yes. For every real y and integer n≥1, x=y/n is real and nx=y.

similar_questions.prompt: Is (ℤ,+) divisible?
similar_questions.solution: No. The equation 2x=1 has no integer solution. Thus the required root exists neither for this y nor for all n.

questions.prompt: f∈ℝ[x] is a product of distinct monic irreducibles P₁,…,Pₙ with n≥2. Which are true about ℝ[x]/(f)?

options.B: It is finite dimensional as an ℝ-vector space
options.C: It is a finite direct sum of fields each isomorphic to ℝ or ℂ
options.D: It has no nonzero nilpotent elements

hints: Apply the Chinese remainder theorem to the pairwise coprime factors.
Real irreducible polynomials have degree one or two.
questions.solution: CRT gives ℝ[x]/(f)≅∏_{i=1}ⁿℝ[x]/(P_i). Each factor is a field, isomorphic to ℝ for a linear factor and ℂ for an irreducible quadratic. Thus C holds; for finite families direct sum and direct product have the same underlying ring. Polynomial division makes the quotient dimension deg f, proving B. If uᵐ=0, each field coordinate has zero mth power and is zero, so u=0, proving D. With n≥2 the product has nonzero zero divisors (coordinate idempotents), hence is not a field and A fails.
questions.theory: Distinct monic irreducible polynomials over a field are pairwise coprime, so their generated ideals are pairwise comaximal. The Chinese remainder theorem identifies the quotient by their product with the finite product of the quotients by each irreducible factor. Each factor quotient is a field. Over ℝ an irreducible polynomial is linear or quadratic; the resulting fields are ℝ and ℂ, respectively. Polynomial division gives a vector-space basis 1,x,…,x^(d−1) for the quotient by a monic degree-d polynomial. A product of two or more nonzero fields has zero divisors but no nonzero nilpotents, because each coordinate field has none. Common pitfalls include calling a product of fields a field and forgetting that repeated factors, unlike distinct factors, can introduce nilpotents.

similar_questions.prompt: Describe ℝ[x]/(x(x−1)).
similar_questions.solution: CRT identifies it with ℝ×ℝ by evaluation at 0 and 1. It has dimension 2, zero divisors, and no nonzero nilpotents.

similar_questions.prompt: Describe ℝ[x]/((x−1)(x²+1)).
similar_questions.solution: The distinct factors are coprime. The quotient is ℝ×ℂ, of real dimension 1+2=3. It is reduced but not a field.

questions.prompt: f(x)=x²⁰²⁵−1 over 𝔽₅. S is its root set in an algebraic closure. Which are true?
hints: Factor the characteristic-power multiplicity from exponent 2025=25·81.
Count distinct roots, then use cyclicity of finite multiplicative field subgroups.
questions.solution: In characteristic five, x²⁰²⁵−1=(x⁸¹−1)²⁵. The derivative of x⁸¹−1 is 81x⁸⁰=x⁸⁰ in 𝔽₅ and never zero at a root, so it has 81 distinct roots in the algebraic closure. They form a finite multiplicative subgroup, hence cyclic. Its generator count is φ(81)=54, whereas φ(2025)=2025(1−1/3)(1−1/5)=1080. Thus A,D hold and B,C fail.
questions.theory: In characteristic p, the Frobenius identity (a−b)^p=a^p−b^p shows that powers divisible by p can create repeated polynomial roots. If m=pᵏd with p not dividing d, then xᵐ−1=(xᵈ−1)^(pᵏ). Its distinct roots are therefore the d roots of xᵈ−1, whose derivative d x^(d−1) is nonzero at each root. These roots form a finite multiplicative subgroup of the field's algebraic closure, and every finite subgroup of a field's multiplicative group is cyclic. A cyclic group of order d has φ(d) generators, distinct from its total d elements. The multiplicative root condition excludes zero. Common pitfalls include equating polynomial degree with the number of distinct roots in positive characteristic and computing generators using the degree before removing the characteristic-power multiplicity.

similar_questions.prompt: How many distinct roots does x¹²−1 have in characteristic 3?
similar_questions.solution: x¹²−1=(x⁴−1)³. Since 3 does not divide 4, x⁴−1 is separable and has four distinct roots in the algebraic closure.

similar_questions.prompt: How many generators do those four roots have?
similar_questions.solution: They form a cyclic group of order 4. Its generator count is φ(4)=2, rather than φ(12)=4.

questions.prompt: On ℝ, U is open iff U=∅ or 0∈U. Which are true?

options.B: For each prime p, {0,√p} is dense

hints: The open singleton {0} tests density.
Cover [0,1] by the open two-point sets {0,x}.
questions.solution: A fails because the nonempty open set {0} misses all irrationals. B holds: every nonempty open set contains 0 and therefore meets {0,√p}. For C, the family {{0,x}:x∈[0,1]} is an open cover with no finite subcover, since a finite union contains only finitely many points. D fails because any two nonempty open neighborhoods share 0, so distinct points cannot have disjoint neighborhoods. Only B holds.
questions.theory: A topology specifies open subsets and thereby determines closure, compactness, separation, and continuity. A subset is dense exactly when it intersects every nonempty open set. In the particular-point topology, every nonempty open set contains a distinguished point; any subset containing that point is dense. The singleton of the distinguished point is open, so a subset missing it cannot be dense. No two nonempty open sets are disjoint, preventing Hausdorff separation in a space with multiple points. Compactness must be checked through finite subcovers, not through Euclidean closedness and boundedness, since the topology has changed. Covering an infinite subset by sets consisting of the distinguished point and one additional point disproves compactness. Common pitfalls include transferring familiar real-line properties to a nonstandard topology and treating density as a metric concept.

similar_questions.prompt: In this topology, characterize all dense subsets.
similar_questions.solution: A dense subset must meet the open singleton {0}, so it must contain 0. Conversely, containing 0 makes it meet every nonempty open set, proving exactly that characterization.

similar_questions.prompt: Which subsets are compact in this topology?
similar_questions.solution: Every finite subset is compact in any topology. An infinite subset has the cover {0,x} indexed by its elements (restricted to the subset); no finite subcover exists. Thus exactly the finite subsets are compact.

questions.prompt: A is homeomorphic to B, B is a dense subspace of C, and C is homeomorphic to a subspace W of A. Which statements are FALSE in general?

options.C: If C is compact, A,B,C are homeomorphic
options.D: If A is connected, B and C are connected

hints: Consider A=B=(0,1), C=[0,1], with a compact subinterval W⊂A.
Connectedness passes through homeomorphism and then to closure.
questions.solution: Take A=B=(0,1), C=[0,1], and W=[1/3,2/3]⊂A. B is dense in C, A≈B, and C≈W by affine scaling. But B is noncompact while W=closure_A(W) and C are compact, so both A and B statements fail. This also disproves C despite its compactness hypothesis. D is true: A connected implies B connected by homeomorphism; C=closure_C(B) is connected because the closure of a connected subset is connected. Therefore the false assertions are A,B,C.
questions.theory: A topological space is connected if it cannot be split into two disjoint nonempty open subsets. Path connectedness requires a continuous path between every pair of points and implies connectedness; the converse fails in general. Open subsets of Euclidean space are locally path connected, so an open connected subset is path connected. Continuous images of connected spaces are connected. For a continuous open surjection with connected fibers, a separation of the domain would induce a separation of the range: each fiber must lie wholly in one side. Compact subsets are closed in Hausdorff spaces, not in arbitrary spaces. A lattice generated by two real-linearly independent complex numbers is discrete rather than dense. Common pitfalls include omitting Hausdorff hypotheses and transferring Euclidean path properties to all topological spaces.

similar_questions.prompt: Can a dense proper subset fail to be homeomorphic to its closure?
similar_questions.solution: Yes. (0,1) is dense in [0,1], but the latter is compact and the former is not. Compactness is preserved by homeomorphism, so they cannot be homeomorphic.

similar_questions.prompt: Prove the closure of a connected subset is connected.
similar_questions.solution: If the closure had a separation into relatively open nonempty U,V, density forces the original subset to meet both. Their intersections would then separate that connected subset, a contradiction.

questions.prompt: y″+5y′+6y=sin(e⁻⁵ˣ), x>0. Which are true?

options.D: Every solution tends to zero as x→∞

hints: The homogeneous roots are −2 and −3.
Use the convolution kernel e⁻²ˣ−e⁻³ˣ and |sin(e⁻⁵ˣ)|≤e⁻⁵ˣ.
questions.solution: Every solution has y=C₁e⁻²ˣ+C₂e⁻³ˣ+∫₀ˣ[e⁻²⁽ˣ⁻ᵗ⁾−e⁻³⁽ˣ⁻ᵗ⁾]sin(e⁻⁵ᵗ)dt, since the coefficients and forcing extend smoothly to zero. The homogeneous terms are bounded and decay. The convolution magnitude is at most ∫₀ˣe⁻²⁽ˣ⁻ᵗ⁾e⁻⁵ᵗdt≤e⁻²ˣ/3, so it is bounded and decays too. Thus A,D hold; B,C contradict this common bound.
questions.theory: A constant-coefficient second-order linear ODE has homogeneous solutions determined by its characteristic roots. Negative real parts give decaying modes. A particular solution for a bounded or decaying forcing can be represented as a convolution with a decaying impulse response; bounding that convolution proves boundedness and decay. For a nonautonomous first-order system, multiplying coordinates by exponential factors can remove time-dependent coefficients and expose a constant matrix. If that matrix is nilpotent, its matrix exponential terminates after finitely many terms. Scalar autonomous equations y′=F(y) can be analyzed using the sign of F and equilibria; uniqueness prevents a trajectory from crossing an equilibrium. Finite-time blow-up follows when ∫^∞dy/F(y) is finite. Common pitfalls include examining only homogeneous solutions, overlooking the maximal existence interval, and assuming smooth polynomial vector fields guarantee global solutions.

similar_questions.prompt: Solve y″+5y′+6y=e⁻⁵ˣ.
similar_questions.solution: The homogeneous solution is C₁e⁻²ˣ+C₂e⁻³ˣ. Try Ae⁻⁵ˣ; substitution gives (25−25+6)A=1, so A=1/6. Every resulting solution is bounded and tends to zero.

similar_questions.prompt: Why can positive-root homogeneous modes destroy boundedness?
similar_questions.solution: For y″−y=0, y=eˣ is a solution and is unbounded. Thus forcing bounds alone do not ensure boundedness unless the homogeneous dynamics are stable.

questions.prompt: u_xx+u_yy=0 on (0,1)², with u(x,0)=eᵖⁱˣ, u(x,1)=−eᵖⁱˣ, u(0,y)=cos(πy)+sin(πy), u(1,y)=eᵖⁱ[cos(πy)+sin(πy)]. Which values occur at an interior point?
hints: Identify a separated harmonic expression meeting all boundary data.
Its exact interior range is between its unattained global extrema.
questions.solution: u(x,y)=e^(πx)[cos(πy)+sin(πy)] satisfies the PDE and all data, so uniqueness identifies it. The bracket ranges from values greater than −1 up to √2; x∈(0,1) gives e^(πx)<eπ. Thus u lies strictly between −eπ and √2eπ, excluding A,D. For B, choose y=1/4 and x=1−log(√2)/π∈(0,1); then u=eπ. For C, choose x=1/2; the bracket continuously varies from √2 to −1 and therefore takes −e^(−π/2), giving u=−1. Hence B,C occur.
questions.theory: The Laplace equation Δu=0 defines harmonic functions; boundary data on a bounded domain determine a unique continuous harmonic solution under the usual classical hypotheses by the maximum principle. Separated functions e^(ax)cos(ay) and e^(ax)sin(ay) are harmonic. For the heat equation u_t=u_xx with zero endpoint data, a sine expansion gives coefficients decaying like e^(−k²π²t), so solutions tend to zero. Uniqueness transfers symmetries of the domain and initial data to the solution. The energy E(t)=∫u² satisfies E′=2∫u u_xx=−2∫u_x² after integration by parts, since the boundary terms vanish. Common pitfalls include claiming interior attainment of a strict boundary maximum, overlooking reflection symmetry, and confusing energy dissipation with pointwise monotonicity.

similar_questions.prompt: Show e^(ax)cos(ay) is harmonic.
similar_questions.solution: Its second x derivative is a²e^(ax)cos(ay), while its second y derivative is −a²e^(ax)cos(ay). Their sum is zero.

similar_questions.prompt: Can a nonconstant harmonic function attain its maximum at an interior point?
similar_questions.solution: No. The strong maximum principle forces a harmonic function attaining an interior maximum to be constant on a connected domain. Thus strict extrema from nonconstant boundary data are not interior values.

questions.prompt: ∫_(x₀)^(x₀+h)f(x)dx≈λh[f(x₀)+f(x₀+h)]+ph³[f″(x₀)+f″(x₀+h)] is exact for the highest possible polynomial degree. Which are true?
hints: Scale to x₀=0,h=1 and test f=1 and f=x².
The resulting rule is also exact for x and x³ but fails at x⁴.
questions.solution: Testing f=1 gives 2λ=1, so λ=1/2. Testing x² gives 1/3=λ+4p, hence p=−1/24. For x and x³, the rule returns 1/2 and λ+6p=1/4, respectively; for x⁴ it returns 1/2−12/24=0 instead of 1/5. Thus degree of exactness is 3 and the coefficients are forced. Then 2λ+24p=1−1=0 and 7λ−12p=7/2+1/2=4. A,B true; C,D false.
questions.theory: A quadrature rule's degree of exactness is the largest polynomial degree for which its output equals the exact integral. Coefficients are determined by testing low-degree monomials, after translating and scaling the integration interval to [0,1]. Derivative-based rules scale a second-derivative term by h³, since two derivatives contribute h⁻². questions.solution: The subtraction gives −x₂=0. Hence x₂=0 and x₁+x₃=1. The third equation becomes (Z₁−1)x₃=Z₂−1. Infinitely many solutions occur exactly when Z₁=1 and Z₂=1; otherwise it is either inconsistent or fixes x₃ uniquely. By independence the probability is [binomial(2,1)(1/2)²]·e⁻¹= e⁻¹/2, B.
questions.theory: Expectation is integration against a probability measure. For independent uniform coordinates on [0,1], an integral over the unit cube is the expectation of the same expression in independent U(0,1) variables. The strong law of large numbers states that sample averages of integrable independent identically distributed variables converge almost surely to their expectations. Ratios converge when the limiting denominator is nonzero. The dominated convergence theorem passes an almost-sure limit through expectation when all random variables are bounded in magnitude by one integrable bound. Bayes' theorem instead combines prior probabilities with conditional likelihoods and normalizes their products. Common pitfalls include dividing expectations instead of applying an asymptotic law, ignoring a zero-denominator point of measure zero, and failing to normalize posterior weights.

questions.solution: Let A₀=∑₁⁸X_i and B₀=∑₈¹³X_i. Their means are 8θ and 6θ, but Cov(A₀,B₀)=Var X₈=θ. Thus E(A₀B₀)=48θ²+θ and A is false. E X_i=θ, so matching the sample mean proves B. questions.theory: A statistic is sufficient for a parameter when the conditional sample distribution given that statistic does not depend on the parameter. The factorization theorem establishes sufficiency by writing the likelihood as a parameter-dependent function of the statistic times a parameter-free factor. Method of moments equates the sample mean to the population mean; for a Poisson model this gives the sample mean as estimator of θ. Overlapping sums are not independent: covariance equals the variance of their shared counts. Exponential-function unbiased estimators can be built using Poisson probability-generating functions or zero-count events. Common pitfalls include assuming different-looking sums are disjoint and confusing a nonlinear transform of a count with loss of information when that transform is injective.

hints: The full-model MLE is the sample maximum M.

questions.solution: For M≤3, Λ=(M/3)³; for M>3 the null likelihood is zero, so rejection is automatic. Under H₀, P(M<c)=(c/3)³, giving the size-0.001 cutoff c=3(0.001)^(1/3)=0.3. Thus reject when M<0.3 or M>3. Values 3.1 and 0.1 reject, while 1.3 does not. At θ=0.3, M<0.3 almost surely, so power is 1. Hence A,C,D hold.
questions.theory: A likelihood-ratio test compares the maximum null likelihood with the maximum likelihood over the full parameter set. Small ratios signal poor agreement with the null. Common pitfalls include designing a symmetric two-tail cutoff and missing automatic rejection when an observation lies outside the null support.

questions.prompt: X_i have density e⁻⁽ˣ⁻ᶿ⁾ for x≥θ, zero otherwise. X_(1)=min X_i. Which intervals have the claimed confidence levels?
hints: The minimum gap has Exp(rate n) distribution.

questions.solution: P(X_(1)−θ>t)=e⁻ⁿᵗ for t≥0. Coverage of (X_(1)−c/n,X_(1)) is P(0<X_(1)−θ<c/n)=1−e⁻ᶜ. With c=2ln5 this is 1−1/25=0.96, so B is true and A false. With c=ln20 it is 1−1/20=0.95, so C is true and D false. Endpoint inclusions do not matter because the pivot is continuous.
questions.theory: A confidence interval is a random interval whose coverage probability equals the stated level for every parameter value. For shifted exponential observations X_i=θ+E_i with E_i iid Exp(1), the minimum gap X_(1)−θ has exponential rate n. Therefore n(X_(1)−θ) is a parameter-free Exp(1) pivot, and an interval (X_(1)−c/n,X_(1)) has coverage 1−e⁻ᶜ. For Uniform(θ,θ+1), the shifted minimum has Beta(1,n) distribution and mean 1/(n+1), so the sample minimum is biased but becomes consistent. Consistency means convergence in probability to the parameter and does not require exact finite-sample unbiasedness. The sample maximum instead converges to θ+1. Common pitfalls include reading a nominal level without calculating its tail probability and confusing asymptotic unbiasedness with exact unbiasedness.

questions.prompt: For a symmetric absolutely continuous sample of size 3, T⁺ is the Wilcoxon sum of positive-sign absolute ranks. Which are true?
hints: Enumerate the eight subsets of ranks {1,2,3}.

questions.solution: The eight equiprobable subset sums are 0,1,2,3,3,4,5,6. Therefore P(T⁺=3)=2/8=1/4, proving A. Write T⁺=B₁+2B₂+3B₃ with iid fair Bernoulli signs; variance=(1+4+9)/4=7/2, proving B. The strict upper tails have P(T⁺>3)=3/8 and P(T⁺>4)=2/8=1/4, rejecting C,D.
questions.theory: The Wilcoxon signed-rank statistic adds the ranks of absolute observations whose signs are positive. Under an absolutely continuous distribution symmetric about zero, ties and zeros occur with probability zero, the signs are independent fair Bernoulli choices, and conditional on the absolute ranks all 2ⁿ subsets of {1,…,n} are equally likely. Thus T⁺ has the distribution of ∑rB_r with independent Bernoulli(1/2) variables. Its mean is n(n+1)/4 and variance n(n+1)(2n+1)/24, obtained by summing r²/4. Exact small-sample probabilities come from enumerating subset sums, with repeated sums counted separately. Common pitfalls include treating the statistic as binomial, counting distinct sums rather than sign patterns, and forgetting that strict tail inequalities exclude the boundary value.

questions.prompt: X_i iid N(θ,1); prior θ~N(1,2). δ_n is the squared-error Bayes estimator. Z is the limit law of [(2n+1)δ_n−1−2nθ]/√n. Which are true?

options.A: δ_n→θ in probability for every θ

hints: Compute the conjugate posterior mean using prior precision 1/2.
The displayed normalized expression simplifies to twice the centered normalized sample sum.
questions.solution: Posterior precision is n+1/2 and mean δ_n=(∑X_i+1/2)/(n+1/2)=(2∑X_i+1)/(2n+1). Its bias is (1−θ)/(2n+1)→0 and variance 4n/(2n+1)²→0, proving A. The normalized expression equals 2(∑X_i−nθ)/√n, exactly N(0,4) for every n. Thus Z~N(0,4), proving B. Its fourth moment is 3·4²=48, proving C, while its second moment is 4, rejecting D.
questions.theory: Under squared-error loss, the Bayes estimator is the posterior mean, assuming the posterior second moment exists. Normal likelihoods and normal priors are conjugate: posterior precision is prior precision plus sample precision, and posterior mean is their precision-weighted combination. For known sampling variance one and prior mean m₀, variance τ², the posterior mean is (nX̄+m₀/τ²)/(n+1/τ²). As sample size increases, prior influence vanishes and the estimator is consistent for each fixed true mean. Exact linear transformations of the sample sum remain normal, so an asymptotic normal law may already hold at every n. A centered normal variable of variance v has second moment v and fourth moment 3v². Common pitfalls include treating prior variance as precision, confusing posterior randomness with frequentist sampling of the estimator, and using standard-normal moments without checking the resulting variance.

similar_questions.solution: Prior precision 1 combines with sample precision n, giving δ=nX̄/(n+1)=∑X_i/(n+1).

questions.prompt: Y_i=β₁+⋯+β_i+ε_i, i=1,…,n, with uncorrelated mean-zero errors of variance σ². β̂_i are BLUEs. Which are true?

options.A: Residual sum of squares is positive almost surely
options.B: Every β_i has infinitely many linear unbiased estimators
options.D: Y₃−Y₂ is the BLUE of β₃

hints: The cumulative-sum design is square and invertible.
Its inverse takes consecutive differences.
questions.solution: The lower-triangular design matrix has ones on and below the diagonal and determinant one. Its inverse yields β̂₁=Y₁ and β̂_i=Y_i−Y_(i−1) for i≥2. The fit is exactly Xβ̂=Y, so residual sum of squares is zero, rejecting A. Any linear unbiased estimator aᵗY of β_i must satisfy aᵗX=e_iᵗ; invertibility makes this solution unique, rejecting B. Var β̂₁=Var ε₁=σ² and β̂₃=Y₃−Y₂, so C,D hold. The source’s β₃ statement naturally presumes n≥3.
questions.theory: In a full-rank normal linear model with k coefficients and n observations, the residual sum of squares Q satisfies Q/σ²~χ²_ν with ν=n−k. The unbiased residual variance estimator is Q/ν, while the maximum-likelihood estimator is Q/n. Since a chi-square variable has mean ν and variance 2ν, these estimators' biases, variances and mean squared errors follow directly. The unbiased estimator has variance 2σ⁴/ν. The MLE has smaller variance 2νσ⁴/n² but downward bias −kσ²/n, so its MSE is σ⁴(2ν+k²)/n². Smaller variance does not automatically imply smaller MSE. For saturated square invertible designs, ν=0 and the fit interpolates the data exactly. Common pitfalls include forgetting the intercept in k and treating equality of MSEs as a strict inequality.

questions.prompt: X₁,X₂ have absolutely continuous laws with hazards h₁(t)≤h₂(t) for all t. Which are true?

options.C: E X₁≥E X₂ if both exist
options.D: h₁+h₂ is the hazard of min(X₁,X₂)

hints: Integrate the hazard inequality to compare survival functions.
The minimum’s hazard sum requires independence, which is absent here.
questions.solution: S_i(t)=exp[−∫_−∞ᵗh_i(s)ds], so h₁≤h₂ implies S₁(t)≥S₂(t), proving A and stochastic ordering. This ordering implies E X₁≥E X₂ whenever both expectations exist, proving C. B fails for X₁~Exp(1), X₂~Exp(3): P(X₁>1)=e⁻¹>e⁻³ᐟ²=P(X₂>1/2). D is not forced without independence: take X₁=X₂~Exp(1). Marginal hazards are both 1, but min equals that same variable and has hazard 1, not 2. Exactly A,C hold.
questions.theory: For an absolutely continuous distribution with survival function S(t)=P(X>t)>0, the hazard is h(t)=f(t)/S(t)=−d log S(t)/dt almost everywhere. Integrating gives S(t)=exp(−∫_−∞ᵗh(s)ds), under the usual endpoint conventions. A smaller hazard therefore gives a larger survival function at every threshold, called first-order stochastic dominance. When expectations exist, this stochastic ordering also orders expectations, either by integrating positive and negative survival tails or by quantile coupling. Hazards add for the minimum of independent lifetimes because its survival function is the product of their survival functions. Without independence, the marginal hazards do not determine the minimum distribution. Common pitfalls include reversing survival ordering, comparing unequal thresholds from a same-threshold theorem, and silently assuming independence.

questions.prompt: Maximize P=x₁+x₂ subject to x₁+x₂+2x₃≤5, 2x₁−3x₃≥1, x₂+x₃≤0, and x₁,x₂,x₃≥0. Which are true?
hints: Nonnegativity and x₂+x₃≤0 force both those coordinates to zero.
Reduce the problem to a one-dimensional interval for x₁.
questions.solution: x₂=x₃=0 follows from the third constraint and nonnegativity. Remaining constraints are x₁≤5 and 2x₁≥1, so the feasible region is {(x₁,0,0):1/2≤x₁≤5}. Its endpoints are the corner points; thus (1/2,0,0) is a corner, proving D. The objective is x₁, maximized at (5,0,0) with value 5, rejecting A,C. Point (4,1,0) violates x₂+x₃≤0, so B fails.
questions.theory: A linear program optimizes a linear objective subject to linear inequalities and, often, nonnegativity restrictions. Its feasible region is a convex polyhedron; an extreme point cannot be expressed as a nontrivial convex combination of two different feasible points. Nonnegativity can make apparently complex constraints force some variables to zero: if x₂,x₃≥0 and x₂+x₃≤0, both must vanish. Reducing the remaining inequalities can reveal a line segment whose endpoints are exactly the corner points. A linear objective on a compact segment attains its optimum at an endpoint, unless it is constant. Every proposed optimal point must first be checked for feasibility, and the objective value should be distinguished from the coordinate vector. Common pitfalls include optimizing over an infeasible point and ignoring the effect of sign constraints.

similar_questions.prompt: Maximize x on the feasible segment 2≤x≤7.
similar_questions.solution: The objective increases with x, so its maximum is 7 at the upper endpoint. The two corner points are 2 and 7.

similar_questions.prompt: If x,y≥0 and x+y≤0, what feasible points exist?
similar_questions.solution: Each nonnegative summand must be zero, so only (0,0) is feasible. This can reduce the dimension of a larger linear program.
